title: Chaos Engineering & SLOs
subtitle: Define how reliable a checkout must be, measure it, spend the error budget on safe failure experiments, and learn from them.
learn: How an SLI, an SLO and an error budget relate to each other
How to turn a 99.9% target into minutes of allowed downtime
Why teams alert on burn rate instead of raw error counts
How to run a chaos experiment with a hypothesis, a small blast radius and an abort rule
How the error budget decides whether to ship, experiment or freeze

steps.title: How reliable is reliable enough?
steps.body: Your checkout service will fail sometimes, because every service it depends on fails sometimes. The useful questions are: how often is failure acceptable, how do we know, and how do we find weak spots before customers do? Asking for 100% is not an answer. Each extra nine costs far more than the last, and users cannot tell the difference past a point.
steps.idea: Reliability is a target you choose and measure, not something you maximise without limit.
steps.caption: Shoppers depend on checkout, which depends on payments and inventory.

steps.title: Measure what users feel
steps.body: A service level indicator (SLI) is a number that says how well the service is doing, usually good events divided by valid events. For checkout, a good event is an order that returns a non-error response (not a 5xx) in under 800 ms. Valid means requests that should count, not health checks or the user's own bad input. Count it at the edge or load balancer, close to the user, and send the result to the metrics store, as the animation shows. CPU and memory are poor SLIs, because a busy server can still serve users fine.
steps.idea: A good SLI is the ratio of good to valid requests, measured as close to the user as practical.
steps.caption: Every request is counted as good or bad and sent to metrics.

steps.title: Set the target and the budget
steps.body: A service level objective (SLO) is the goal for the SLI over a time window. Say checkout must be good for 99.9% of requests over 30 days. The other 0.1% is the error budget, the amount of badness you may spend. A 30-day window is 43,200 minutes, so 0.1% is about 43 minutes of full outage, or the same amount spread across partial failures. The budget is not a failure. It is room to ship changes and take risks.
steps.idea: SLO = target for the SLI. Error budget = 100% minus the SLO, as allowed badness.
steps.caption: Target 99.9% over 30 days leaves about 43 minutes of budget.

steps.title: An outage spends the budget
steps.body: Earlier this month a bad deploy made payments fail for 13 minutes. Every checkout in that window was a bad event. With steady traffic, about 13 of the 43 budget minutes are gone and the 30-day SLI is now about 99.97%. About 30 minutes remain. The budget turns a vague 'we had a rough month' into a number that engineers and product owners can both read.
steps.idea: Every bad minute is a withdrawal. The remaining budget says how much risk you can still afford.
steps.caption: Payments failed for 13 minutes; budget drops to 30.

steps.title: Alert on how fast you burn
steps.body: Paging on every error is noisy. Paging only when the budget is gone is too late. Burn rate is the actual error rate divided by the allowed error rate. If 1.44% of requests fail against a 0.1% budget, the burn rate is 14.4. At that speed the whole 30-day budget is gone in about 50 hours, and 2% of it burns in one hour. A common pattern is to page on a fast burn (around 14x over an hour) and open a ticket on a slow burn (around 1x over a few days). Checking a long and a short window together lets alerts clear quickly after a fix.
steps.idea: Burn rate says how long until the budget is gone, so alerts can match urgency.
steps.caption: A fast burn pages the on-call engineer.

steps.title: Break it on purpose, with a hypothesis
steps.body: Chaos engineering means injecting real failure on purpose to test whether the system behaves as you believe. Start with a steady state, the normal you can measure: 'checkout p99 stays under 800 ms and success stays above 99.9%'. Checkout p99 is about 450 ms today. Hypothesis: 'if payments gets 300 ms slower, checkout still meets both', since 450 + 300 = 750 ms. Faults can be delay, errors, killed instances or blocked dependencies. Here the chaos tool adds the delay and watches the same SLI. It is an experiment, not vandalism.
steps.idea: A chaos experiment tests a written hypothesis against a measurable steady state.
steps.caption: The chaos tool adds 300 ms of delay to payments.

steps.title: Keep the blast radius small
steps.body: Blast radius is how many users and systems an experiment can hurt. Begin with the smallest slice that still teaches you something: one instance, one test account or 1% of traffic, for a few minutes, off peak but with owners at their desks. In the animation only 1% of checkouts take the slowed path. Widen only after each smaller run passes. Staging is good for finding tooling bugs, but it rarely has real traffic, so many lessons only show up in production, once monitoring and an abort switch are in place.
steps.idea: Start tiny, widen step by step, and never expand while a run is failing.
steps.caption: Only 1% of checkouts go through the delayed payments path.

steps.title: The experiment finds a weakness
steps.body: At 1% the hypothesis holds. At 5%, the slow charges hold on to connections and threads longer. The connection pool to payments (a fixed set of reusable connections) fills up, requests queue, and some pass 800 ms and count as bad. The cause: the call has no tight timeout or fallback, so checkout waits instead of failing fast or accepting the order and retrying the charge later. This planned test costs well under a tenth of a minute of budget, which a 2 a.m. incident would not.
steps.idea: A failed hypothesis is a win: you found the flaw cheaply and on your own schedule.
steps.caption: At 5% blast radius, slow payments push checkout past 800 ms.

steps.title: Abort rules and game days
steps.body: Every experiment needs an automatic stop. For example, abort if burn exceeds 3x over a few minutes, or if the SLI drops below a floor, and the chaos tool removes the fault at once. Guardrails use a short window, unlike hour-long paging windows. Here burn reaches 5x within a couple of minutes at 5%, so the tool halts the run. A game day is a scheduled team exercise: several experiments run together with owners watching and a rollback plan ready, and notes written afterwards.
steps.idea: Safe chaos has a kill switch tied to the same SLI that defines normal.
steps.caption: Burn limit crossed, the chaos tool stops injecting.

steps.title: Measure, spend, test, learn
steps.body: An SLI measures what users feel, an SLO sets the target, and the error budget is what remains to spend. Burn-rate alerts say how urgent a problem is. Chaos experiments test a hypothesis with a small blast radius and an abort rule, and game days practise this as a team. A simple policy: with plenty of budget, ship and experiment. When it is nearly spent, ship only low-risk changes and pause new experiments (chaos runs spend budget too). At zero, freeze feature launches until the window recovers. The thresholds are a team choice.
steps.idea: Reliability is managed like money: set a budget, track it, and spend it on learning.
steps.caption: The full loop from metric to experiment.

quiz.q: Your SLO is 99.9% good requests over 30 days. About how much full-outage time does the error budget allow?
options: About 4 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 7 hours
About 43 hours
quiz.why: 30 days is 43,200 minutes. 0.1% of that is about 43 minutes. 99.99% would give about 4 minutes, and 99% about 7 hours.

quiz.q: Which is the best SLI for a checkout API?
options: Average CPU use across servers
Number of servers running
Share of order requests that succeed in under 800 ms
Total requests per day
quiz.why: A good SLI is a ratio of good to valid events measured from the user's side. CPU, server count and raw volume do not say whether users were served well.

quiz.q: An alert shows a burn rate of 14.4 against a 30-day SLO. What does that mean?
options: The budget will last about 50 hours if this continues
14.4% of requests are failing
The budget lasts 14.4 days
The SLO is 14.4 nines
quiz.why: Burn rate is the actual error rate divided by the allowed error rate. At 14.4x, 30 days divided by 14.4 is about 2 days, so roughly 50 hours.

quiz.q: You want to test how checkout copes with slow payments. Which plan is safest and most useful?
options: Slow payments for all users at peak time, to see real impact
Run it only in staging and assume production behaves the same
Slow 1% of traffic briefly, auto-stop if the SLI breaches a floor
Kill payments entirely and watch what the on-call does
quiz.why: State a hypothesis, start with a small blast radius, watch the steady-state SLI, and stop automatically on breach. Staging alone misses real traffic, and full outages at peak are reckless.

quiz.q: Mid-month the error budget is almost used up. What does a sensible error-budget policy do?
options: Raise the SLO so the numbers look better
Pause risky launches and chaos runs, and prioritise reliability work
Ignore it until the window resets
Add alerts on every single error
quiz.why: The budget's job is to steer trade-offs. When it is nearly spent, the team slows risk-taking and fixes reliability until the window recovers.

cheatsheet.def: Service level indicator: a measured ratio of good events to valid events, such as fast successful checkouts over all checkouts.
Service level objective: the target for an SLI over a window, for example 99.9% over 30 days.
Service level agreement: a contract with consequences, often refunds, if a promised level is missed. Usually looser than the internal SLO.

100% minus the SLO. At 99.9% over 30 days it is about 43 minutes of full outage, available to spend on risk. A policy ties it to action: ship and experiment while plenty is left, slow down when nearly spent, freeze launches at zero.
Actual error rate divided by allowed error rate. 1x spends the budget exactly over the window; 14.4x empties it in about 50 hours.
The measurable normal behaviour, such as the SLI staying above target, that a chaos experiment tries to keep intact.
How many users or systems an experiment can affect. Start small, such as 1% of traffic, and widen only after passing.
A planned team exercise that runs failure experiments with owners watching, an abort plan and a written follow-up.
